video.title: Data poisoning and backdoors: Attacks through training data
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Charts draw themselves; code is typed out on a card, left to right in both languages. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.

Dr Joseph - computer science lecturer, Nairobi
Narrator - the Darsi voice, talking to a university lecturer (warm, collegial, precise)

chapters.label: The chatbot that learned too fast

scenes.narration: In 2016 a company launched a chatbot that learned from conversations with the public. Within a day, coordinated users had taught it offensive replies, and it was taken offline. Nobody hacked the code. They fed it data.
Today: how attackers change a model by changing its training data, the difference between availability, targeted and backdoor poisoning, and how to teach data provenance as a security control.
Data poisoning means inserting or changing training examples so that the trained model behaves as the attacker wants. Any model trained on scraped, crowdsourced or user data is exposed.

Availability attacks lower accuracy for everyone. Targeted attacks make the model fail on chosen inputs. Backdoor attacks plant a hidden trigger, such as a small patch, that switches the output only when it appears.
Add a small yellow square to one percent of stop sign photos and label them as speed limits. The model stays accurate on clean tests, so nobody notices. With the square, it reads a speed limit.
Defences start before training. Track where every data source comes from, limit who can add data, filter outliers, and keep a trusted held-out set. Clean accuracy alone cannot reveal a backdoor.
Students treat datasets as fixed and trustworthy. Ask them to draw the full data supply chain of a model, from collection to labelling to download, and mark where an attacker could insert examples.
Quick check! A model is accurate on clean tests but misreads any image with a small yellow square. Which kind of poisoning is this?
A backdoor. The trigger switches the output, and clean accuracy hides it.
In the app, open the poison lab. Add poisoned points to the training set, retrain, and watch the decision boundary move.
Your turn. A team trains on images scraped from the web. Which step best protects it against poisoning?
Provenance tracking with filtering and a trusted test set. Remember: poisoning attacks the data, backdoors hide behind clean accuracy, and defence starts in the data supply chain.

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct: a hidden trigger planted through training data.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite: accuracy is fine, and the trigger was learned in training.
